01Part One

What Is Electricity?

Electricity is not magic, even though it can feel that way. A switch flips, a room lights up. A charger plugs in, and a dead tablet wakes up. A storm cloud cracks open the sky with lightning. Underneath all of that is one big idea.

Electricity has to do with electric charge.

The U.S. Department of Energy describes electricity as the flow of electrical charge and one of the most widely used forms of energy in our world. The U.S. Energy Information Administration calls electricity a , meaning humans usually make electricity by converting another energy source like coal, natural gas, sunlight, wind, falling water, or nuclear energy.

Electricity shows up in two major ways:

TypeWhat HappensExample
Static electricityCharge builds up in one placeBalloon sticks to a wall
Current electricityCharge moves through a pathPhone charger powering a phone
Stop and Think
Why is electricity useful only when it can be controlled?
Uncontrolled electricity (like lightning) is unpredictable and dangerous. To use it for lights, computers, or refrigerators, we need it to flow exactly where we want, at the right strength, and only when we want it to. Wires, switches, and circuits let us steer that flow.

Why is electricity called a "secondary energy source"?
02Part Two

Atoms, Protons,
Electrons and Charge

To understand electricity, you have to start smaller than wires, batteries, or phones. You have to start with atoms.

Everything around you is made of : air, water, metal, wood, your desk, your skin, and the wires inside the wall. Atoms are the tiny building blocks of matter, and they are themselves made of even smaller particles.

↑ Click any particle to learn about it

ParticleChargeLocation in Atom
ProtonPositive (+)Nucleus (center)
NeutronNeutral (no charge)Nucleus (center)
ElectronNegative (−)Orbiting around the nucleus

Electricity mostly depends on and . There is a simple rule that matters more than almost anything else in this lesson:

Opposite Charges Attract.
Like Charges Repel.

That means a positive and a negative charge pull toward each other. Two positives push apart. Two negatives push apart. Electrons are also much easier to move than protons. Protons are locked inside the nucleus. Electrons, especially in some materials, can hop from atom to atom. That hopping is what creates electric current.

Stop and Think
If electrons are negative and protons are positive, what would happen if a negatively charged object came near a positively charged object?
They would be attracted to each other and pull toward each other, because opposite charges attract.
Quick CheckSection 2 Check
Why are electrons more important than protons in producing electric current?

Static Electricity

happens when electric charge builds up on a surface instead of flowing in a circuit. You have probably felt it before:

  • Your hair stands up after rubbing a balloon on it.
  • You touch a doorknob and feel a tiny shock.
  • Clothes stick together coming out of a dryer.
  • A balloon sticks to a wall after you rub it on your sweater.

When two materials rub against each other, electrons may move from one to the other. One object gains extra electrons and becomes negatively charged. The other loses electrons and becomes positively charged. That charge imbalance creates pull or push.

A neutral balloon has equal positive and negative charges.
After rubbing, try sticking the balloon here.
Stop and Think
Why are static shocks more noticeable with metal doorknobs than with wooden doors?
Metal lets electric charge move easily, so the built-up charge on your body can rush quickly into the metal as a small spark. Wood resists the movement of charge, so the buildup leaks away slowly and you don't feel a sudden zap.

04Part Four

Current Electricity
and the Circuit

Static electricity is charge waiting around, then suddenly jumping. Current electricity is charge moving in a steady path through a wire.

A is the flow of electric charge. In metal wires, current usually means electrons moving through the material. Current electricity is what powers lights, computers, refrigerators, game systems, and most of the technology around you.

But current needs a road to travel on. That road is called a : a complete loop that starts at an energy source, goes through wires and devices, and comes back to where it started.

Build a Circuit. Flip the Switch.

Switch OFF

A circuit has four important parts. The flashlight in your house is a great example.

Circuit PartWhat It DoesFlashlight Example
Energy sourcePushes charges through the circuitBattery
Conductive pathCarries the electric currentMetal strips or wires
LoadUses the electrical energy to do workThe bulb or LED
SwitchOpens or closes the circuitThe on/off button

Open. Closed. Short.

When the switch is closed, the path is complete. Current can flow and the bulb lights up. When the switch is open, the path is broken. Current cannot flow, and the bulb stays dark. A happens when current finds a path with almost no resistance, like a bare wire from the + to − side of a battery. That is dangerous because the current rushes through and can cause sparks, fires, or burns.

Stop and Think
A flashlight has a battery and a bulb. Why does it also need metal pieces or wires inside?
The metal pieces and wires are the conductive path. Without them, electrons would have no way to travel from the battery to the bulb and back. The circuit would be broken before it even started.
Quick CheckSection 4 Check
What happens in an open circuit?
05Part Five

Energy
Transforms

Electricity is useful because it can change into other kinds of energy. The lamp on your desk doesn't just sit there: electrical energy walks into it, and light and heat walk out.

This change is called energy transformation: energy moving from one form into another. National Geographic describes it as the change of energy from one form into another. Electricity does not vanish when you use it. It transforms.

🍞Toaster
📱Phone
⚙Motor
📦Microwave

Click any device above to see how it transforms electrical energy.

Notice something? Almost every device produces some heat as a side effect, even when heat isn't the goal. A phone gets warm. A lamp's bulb gets hot. That heat is energy that wasn't quite captured as useful output. This is why energy efficiency matters.

Stop and Think
When a video game console is running, what forms of energy does the electrical energy become?
Light (the screen and indicator LEDs), sound (the speakers or controller rumble), heat (the console gets warm and the fan kicks on), and motion (a spinning fan or a vibrating controller). It even sends out tiny electromagnetic signals to a wireless controller.

06Part Six

Conductors
vs Insulators

Not every material moves electricity the same way. Some practically welcome electrons through. Others build a wall.

A lets electric charge move easily. Metals are usually great conductors because some of their electrons can drift freely from atom to atom. That is why wires are made of copper or aluminum. An resists the flow of charge. Rubber, plastic, and dry wood block current. That is why the outside of a cord is plastic. The inside metal moves electricity; the outside plastic keeps it from leaking into your hand.

Test the Materials

Click any material to test it in this circuit. Will the bulb light up?

Click a material to test it.

Water is tricky. Pure water doesn't conduct very well. But the water in your sink, the pool, the puddle, and your skin all contain dissolved minerals or salts. That makes them conduct electricity surprisingly well. This is why mixing water and electricity is so dangerous.

Stop and Think
Why do electrical cords have metal inside but plastic or rubber outside?
The metal inside is a conductor that lets the electric current travel where it needs to go. The plastic or rubber outside is an insulator that keeps the current from leaking out into your hand, into other wires, or into anything else nearby. The two materials work together: one carries, one contains.
Quick CheckSection 6 Check

07Part Seven

Voltage,
Current, Resistance

Three measurements come up over and over again when people talk about electricity. They have a relationship as predictable as water flowing through a pipe.

TermSimple MeaningWater Comparison
VoltageThe electric pushWater pressure in the pipe
CurrentThe amount of charge flowingWater flowing through the pipe
ResistanceHow much something opposes the flowA narrow or blocked pipe

Adjust the Knobs. Watch the Current Change.

5 V
1 Ω
Resulting Current 5.0 A

When you raise voltage, the push gets stronger and more current flows. When you raise resistance, the path gets harder to move through and current drops. There is even a famous law that ties these together: Current = Voltage ÷ Resistance. You don't have to memorize that yet, but you just figured out the pattern by playing with the sliders.

Stop and Think
If a wire has very high resistance, what would happen to the current flowing through it?
The current would drop. High resistance is like a narrow or blocked pipe: even with strong pressure (voltage), only a small amount can squeeze through. Some of the energy that doesn't get through gets converted to heat instead.
Quick CheckSection 7 Check
In the water analogy, what does voltage represent?
08Part Eight

Series
vs Parallel

Circuits can be wired in two different ways, and the choice makes a huge difference in how things work.

A has only one path for current. Picture a single line of bulbs strung along a wire. If one bulb burns out, the path is broken and they all go dark.

A has more than one path. Each device has its own branch. If one bulb breaks, the others still work, because the other branches are still complete loops.

Try Breaking a Bulb in Each Type

Click any bulb to break it. Watch what happens.

This is why your house uses parallel circuits. If everything was in series, then unplugging your toaster would also turn off the refrigerator, the lights, the TV, and everything else. With parallel wiring, every outlet and every appliance has its own loop back to the source.

Stop and Think
Why would a house be a bad place to use only one giant series circuit?
Because the moment any single device broke or was unplugged, the entire house would lose power. The refrigerator, lights, internet, fans, and everything else would all shut off together. Parallel wiring lets each appliance work independently.
Quick CheckSection 8 Check
In a series circuit with three bulbs, what happens if you remove the middle bulb?
09Part Nine

Electricity Meets
Magnetism

Here is one of the strangest, most powerful facts in all of physics: electricity and magnetism are two faces of the same thing.

When electric current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire. If you wrap that wire into a coil and stick an iron nail in the middle, you have built an : a magnet that you can turn on and off with the flip of a switch. The more current, the stronger the magnet.

Build an Electromagnet

0 A
No current. The nail is just a nail.

Motors and Generators

Electromagnetism gives us two of the most important inventions in human history:

  • A uses electricity and magnetism to create motion. (Fan, blender, electric car, drill, robot.)
  • A uses motion and magnetism to create electricity. (Power plants run on these.)

That last sentence is one of the most important in this whole lesson. Almost all electricity in your house comes from spinning a generator. Whether the spin is powered by burning coal, falling water, splitting atoms, or blowing wind, the final step is the same: motion turns a magnet inside a coil, and electric current pops out the other end.

Stop and Think
Why is it useful for an electromagnet to be able to turn on and off, unlike a regular permanent magnet?
You can pick something up with an electromagnet and then drop it on command, just by turning off the current. That is why junkyards use giant electromagnets to lift scrap metal: the crane grabs the metal, swings it over a different pile, then shuts off the electromagnet and the metal drops. A permanent magnet would never let go.
Quick CheckSection 9 Check
What does a generator do?
10Part Ten

How We
Make Electricity

Most power plants work the same basic way: take some kind of energy, use it to spin a turbine, and let the turbine spin a generator.

The fuels and methods differ, but the heart of almost every power plant is the same: motion creates magnetism, and magnetism creates electric current. The only major exception is solar, where light is turned directly into electricity without any spinning at all.

Compare the Sources

🔥Fossil Fuel
Coal & Gas

Burn fuel to boil water. Steam spins the turbine. Releases carbon dioxide and other pollution.

☢Nuclear
Nuclear

Split uranium atoms. The fission releases huge heat. Steam spins turbines. Very low carbon, but creates radioactive waste.

💧Renewable
Hydroelectric

Falling water spins turbines. Renewable and clean, but dams can change rivers and harm wildlife.

💨Renewable
Wind

Wind pushes blades, which spin a generator. No fuel needed. Only works when the wind blows.

☀Renewable
Solar

Photovoltaic cells turn sunlight directly into electricity. No turbine needed at all.

🌋Renewable
Geothermal

Heat from inside Earth creates steam that spins turbines. Works best where underground heat is easy to reach.

The Electric Grid

Electricity doesn't just appear at the outlet. It travels a long way through a system called the . From the power plant, electricity moves through high-voltage transmission lines, then steps down at substations, then arrives at your neighborhood through distribution lines, then enters your home at a voltage that is safe to use. High voltage is used for long-distance travel because it loses less energy on the way. Near your home, transformers lower it to a safer level.

Stop and Think
Most power plants use turbines and generators. Which power source above does not always need a spinning turbine?
Solar. Photovoltaic panels turn sunlight directly into electricity using special materials, with no turbine spinning at all. (Some big solar plants do use the sun's heat to make steam and spin turbines, but most rooftop and farm-style solar panels go directly from light to current.)
Quick CheckSection 10 Check
In a coal-fired power plant, what is the role of the steam?
11Part Eleven

Electricity
Is Dangerous

The same thing that makes electricity so useful (it transfers energy fast and easily) is what makes it dangerous. If current flows through a human body, it can cause shocks, burns, muscle injury, heart problems, or death.

The Electrical Safety Foundation International tells people to stay at least 35 feet from any downed power line and to always assume a downed line is energized. The National Fire Protection Association warns to keep cords away from children, avoid overloading outlets, and use a special safety outlet called a in any room where water might be near electricity.

Top 10 Safety Rules

  1. Never put objects into outlets.
  2. Keep water away from electrical devices.
  3. Do not touch electrical items with wet hands.
  4. Do not overload outlets or power strips.
  5. Stay at least 35 feet away from downed power lines.
  6. Do not use damaged cords.
  7. Use adult help with plugs, cords, and appliances.
  8. Keep metal away from outlets and battery terminals.
  9. Do not yank cords from the wall.
  10. Respect every warning label.

12Part Twelve

Save
Some Electrons

Energy conservation means reducing the energy we waste. It doesn't mean never using electricity. It means using it carefully.

Every watt of electricity has to come from somewhere. If you waste less, the power plants behind your wall have to make less, which means less fuel burned, less land used, and less pollution released. Small choices in a million houses add up to a real difference.

There's also a difference between two related ideas:

IdeaWhat It MeansExample
ConservationUsing less energy by changing your behaviorTurning off lights when you leave a room
EfficiencyUsing better technology to do the same job with less energyReplacing an old bulb with an LED

Stop and Think
Which saves energy by behavior: turning off a lamp, or replacing it with an LED bulb?
Turning off a lamp is conservation, because it's a change in what you do. Replacing it with an LED is efficiency, because it's a change in the equipment. Both save energy, but in different ways.

14 Big Ideas
to Remember

Before the final assessment, here are the most important ideas from this lesson. Read each one. If any feel fuzzy, scroll back to that section before you take the quiz.

01

Electricity is connected to electric charge.

02

03

Opposite charges attract. Like charges repel.

04

Static electricity is charge buildup. Current electricity is charge moving.

05

A circuit must be complete for current to flow.

06

Conductors let current move easily. Insulators resist it.

07

Voltage pushes. Current is the flow. Resistance slows it down.

08

Series circuits have one path. Parallel circuits have many.

09

Electricity and magnetism are deeply connected.

10

Generators turn motion into electricity.

11

Most electricity is made by transforming another energy source.

12

Electrical energy can transform into light, heat, sound, motion, and more.

13

Electricity is dangerous because it transfers energy quickly.

14

Conservation means reducing waste. Efficiency means using less to do the same job.
